analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain to oil and gas drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, never advanced past its committee referral and died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, leaving the Arctic refuge's coastal plain closed to drilling.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have repealed the legal prohibition on drilling for oil and gas in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain, a roughly 1.5-million-acre area in Alaska, and set up a competitive leasing program there. It required the Interior Department to hold the first lease sale within 22 months and capped the total surface footprint of development at 2,000 acres, with seasonal limits on exploration to protect caribou calving and other wildlife. It would also have made it much harder to challenge the drilling program in court: complaints would have had to be filed within 90 days, in one specific appeals court, and the Interior Secretary's environmental analysis would be presumed correct unless opponents proved otherwise. Half the leasing revenue would have gone to Alaska, with a small capped fund for affected local communities and land conveyances to Alaska Native corporations.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain access to federal leases on the refuge's coastal plain, with a guaranteed first sale of at least 200,000 acres within 22 months. The State of Alaska would receive 50% of all bonus, rental, and royalty revenue. Alaska Native corporations (Arctic Slope Regional Corporation and Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation) would receive land conveyances and hiring preferences. North Slope communities would get a capped impact-aid fund for services like firefighting, water, and medical support.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil companies, Alaska's treasury, Native corporations

how_it_helps.text: It would have opened the refuge's coastal plain to oil and gas drilling under a competitive leasing program, with a first lease sale required within 22 months of enactment covering at least 200,000 acres of the most promising tracts.

It would have repealed the 1980 law's prohibition on producing oil and gas from the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and made that repeal the Interior Secretary's only authority to close any of the coastal plain to drilling.

It would have speeded development by requiring the first lease sale within 22 months, capping the total surface footprint of production facilities at 2,000 acres, and directing the Secretary to consider only a leasing plan rather than any no-drilling alternative.

It would have sent 50% of leasing and royalty revenue to the State of Alaska, capped a local impact-aid fund at $11 million for affected Alaska communities, and conveyed land to the Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and Arctic Slope Regional Corporation.

It included some environmental conditions on drilling: a no-significant-adverse-effect standard for fish, wildlife, and subsistence resources, seasonal limits on exploration, reclamation liability for lessees, and a requirement that lessees negotiate project labor agreements and make best efforts to hire Alaska Natives.

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the loss of the coastal plain's undeveloped state — risks to caribou, migratory birds, polar bears, and subsistence hunting grounds — and would face a system deliberately narrowed to make court challenges difficult. Taxpayers would forego any alternative use of the refuge. Future Congresses would lose the ability to close areas to drilling, since the bill would make the Secretary's leasing decisions effectively the final word.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have opened roughly 1.5 million acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain to oil and gas leasing, permanently ending the area's protection from development.

It would have sharply limited the ability of citizens to challenge the drilling program in court: complaints had to be filed within 90 days, only in the D.C. federal appeals court, the Interior Secretary's environmental analysis would be presumed correct unless disproven by clear and convincing evidence, and the Secretary's actions could not be raised later in any enforcement proceeding.

The bill would have narrowed environmental review: the Interior Secretary would not have to study any non-leasing alternative before the first lease sale, and would only consider public comments filed within 20 days on the agency's preferred plan.

An honest supporter would concede that the bill's headline benefits for consumers were speculative: the oil would take years to reach market, and the bill contained no provision guaranteeing lower prices, only a ban on exporting the oil produced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's supporters could honestly point to real safeguards: a 2,000-acre development footprint cap, seasonal drilling limits, a 12.5% royalty, an export ban, reclamation liability, project labor agreements, and impact aid for local communities. But the core trade it offered was permanent industrial development of a pristine section of a wildlife refuge, and its enforcement structure — a 90-day filing window, review confined to the D.C. appeals court, a presumption that the Interior Secretary's analysis was correct, and a bar on raising the law in enforcement cases — made those safeguards much harder to actually enforce. On balance, the bill's design prioritized getting leases sold quickly over protecting the refuge or giving opponents a fair day in court.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House committee that handles natural resources and sat there, with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action, until the two-year Congress ended and it expired.

narrative.text: Representative Richard Pombo introduced the bill on June 4, 2004, in the final session of the 108th Congress.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Resources; that was the only action the bill ever received.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor — the bill had zero.
The committee never reported the bill to the House, and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, so the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Arctic refuge's coastal plain stayed closed to drilling, preserving the area for wildlife, subsistence users, and future public decisions. Oil and gas companies lost the chance at new federal leases.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The refuge and the publics that value it

for.name: Richard W. Pombo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to open the Arctic refuge's coastal plain to oil and gas leasing.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and no member of either party signed on as a cosponsor, so the bill's support in Congress is visible only as its single Republican sponsor.

industries.note: The bill's central purpose was to give oil and gas companies access to roughly 1.5 million acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain, ending the 1980 prohibition on drilling there. Its short court deadlines and narrow review rules would have made it harder for opponents to slow or stop leases, which is where the industry's interest runs against the public's interest in keeping the refuge undeveloped.

industries.industry: Alaska Native regional and village corporations (Arctic Slope Regional Corporation, Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation)
industries.note: The bill would have conveyed surface and subsurface land to these corporations and required lessees to make best efforts to hire Alaska Natives, giving them both assets and a role in development. Whether this helps ordinary people depends on the community: it creates ownership stakes and jobs tied to a project many Alaska Native and Gwich'in communities oppose for subsistence reasons.

The bill would have required project labor agreements for construction on the leases, channeling work to union-signatory contractors and workers. That provision favors organized construction labor but only to the extent the drilling it enables proceeds.

industries.industry: North Slope local governments (North Slope Borough, city of Kaktovik)
industries.note: Local governments would have received impact-aid grants from a fund capped at $11 million to cover firefighting, water, medical, and other service costs from drilling. The aid is small relative to the industrial activity it offsets, and the communities would bear the on-the-ground effects of development.
